lessons.title: The Three-Limit Rule: How the Tax-Free Part of HRA Is Worked Out

body.text: The tax-free part of your HRA is always the smallest of three numbers. Once you know which of the three is the smallest for you, you know what actually controls your exemption, and what changing it would take.

children.text: Most people treat HRA as a black box: HR enters some numbers, a figure appears on the payslip. But the rule under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 11) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10(13A) of the 1961 Act), read with Rule 279 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026, is short enough to do on a phone calculator. This lesson takes each limit apart, then shows you how to spot which one is holding your exemption down.
The Rule in One Line

body.caption: H = HRA received, R = rent actually paid, S = salary (basic + eligible DA + fixed-percentage commission), p = 50% in the eight listed cities or 40% elsewhere. All measured for the same period.

markDefs.definition: The part of House Rent Allowance that is not exempt. It is added to your taxable salary and taxed at your slab rate.

children.text: Whatever is left of your HRA after the exemption, H minus the exempt amount, is
taxable HRA
and is added to your salary income. If Limit 2 comes out negative because your rent is less than 10% of salary, it is treated as zero, and so is your exemption.
Each Limit, and What It Is Really Saying
Limit 1: HRA actually received

You cannot exempt more HRA than you were paid. However high your rent, the tax-free amount is capped at the HRA your employer credited. This is why an employee paying ₹60,000 a month rent on ₹20,000 of HRA gets no more than ₹20,000 a month exempt.
Limit 2: Rent paid minus 10% of salary

The law assumes you would spend about 10% of your salary on housing anyway, and only gives relief for rent above that. This is the only limit that moves with your rent. Every extra rupee of rent raises Limit 2 by a rupee, which is why Limit 2 is so often the smallest for people in modest flats or shared homes.
Limit 3: 50% or 40% of salary

A ceiling tied to your pay, not your rent. It stops very high HRA packages from becoming almost fully tax-free. It depends on the city where your rented home is situated: 50% in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad from tax year 2026-27, and 40% everywhere else.
The Binding Limit

markDefs.definition: The smallest of the three HRA limits in your case. It decides your exemption, and only a change to that limit, not the other two, can increase it.

children.text: The limit that turns out smallest is your
binding limit
. It tells you what is capping your exemption. Here are four real-world patterns, one for each outcome.

body.caption: Four employees, four different binding limits (annual figures, tax year 2026-27)

cells: None: rent is below 10% of salary

body.title: Show me the working for all four

children.text: Divya, Bengaluru (50%). Salary ₹7,20,000. Limit 1: ₹2,88,000. Limit 2: ₹4,20,000 minus ₹72,000 = ₹3,48,000. Limit 3: 50% of ₹7,20,000 = ₹3,60,000. Smallest is Limit 1, so all ₹2,88,000 of her HRA is exempt. She pays more rent than the HRA can cover.

Rohit, Chennai (50%). Salary ₹6,00,000. Limit 1: ₹3,00,000. Limit 2: ₹1,80,000 minus ₹60,000 = ₹1,20,000. Limit 3: ₹3,00,000. Smallest is Limit 2, so ₹1,20,000 is exempt and ₹1,80,000 is taxable. His rent is low relative to his HRA.

Aisha, Lucknow (40%). Salary ₹6,00,000. Limit 1: ₹3,00,000. Limit 2: ₹3,60,000 minus ₹60,000 = ₹3,00,000. Limit 3: 40% of ₹6,00,000 = ₹2,40,000. Smallest is Limit 3, so ₹2,40,000 is exempt and ₹60,000 is taxable. Her employer pays HRA at 50% of basic, but Lucknow is a 40% city.

Manish, Indore (40%). Salary ₹12,00,000. Limit 2: ₹96,000 minus ₹1,20,000 is negative, so it is zero. His exemption is nil and all ₹4,80,000 of HRA is taxable, even though he pays rent. A ₹8,000 PG bed on a ₹1 lakh basic salary is below the 10% threshold.

body.title: Quick Check: Spot the Binding Limit
body.question: Pooja lives in Kochi and is on the old regime. Her basic is ₹40,000 a month, her HRA is ₹20,000 a month and she pays ₹22,000 a month in rent. Which limit binds?
body.explanation: Annual salary is ₹4,80,000. Limit 1 is ₹2,40,000. Limit 2 is ₹2,64,000 minus ₹48,000 = ₹2,16,000. Limit 3: Kochi is not one of the eight cities, so 40% of ₹4,80,000 = ₹1,92,000. The smallest is Limit 3, so ₹1,92,000 is exempt and ₹48,000 is taxable. Paying more rent would not help her at all.

children.text: How Rent Moves Your Exemption
Take Divya: basic ₹60,000 a month, HRA ₹24,000 a month, living in Bengaluru. Watch what happens to her annual exemption as her monthly rent rises.

body.title: Divya's annual exempt HRA at different monthly rents

children.text: Three zones show up. Below ₹6,000 a month, her rent does not cross 10% of salary and the exemption is zero. From ₹6,000 to ₹30,000, every extra ₹1,000 of monthly rent adds ₹12,000 of annual exemption, because Limit 2 is binding. Above ₹30,000, the line goes flat: she has hit Limit 1 and has no more HRA to exempt.

body.label: Rent ceiling: the rent above which the exemption stops growing
body.value: Smaller of Limit 1 and Limit 3, plus 10% of salary
body.context: For Divya: ₹2,88,000 plus ₹72,000 = ₹3,60,000 a year, or ₹30,000 a month. Any rent above this adds nothing to her exemption.

body.text: Tax exemptions never make spending profitable. Even in the 30% slab, each extra rupee of rent below the ceiling saves you at most 31.2 paise of tax, including cess. Above the ceiling it saves nothing. Choose the flat you want to live in, then optimise the paperwork.

body.title: Scenario: Upgrading the Flat for Tax Reasons
body.scenario: Divya currently pays ₹30,000 a month for a 1BHK in HSR Layout. A friend tells her to move to a ₹38,000 2BHK because "higher rent means more HRA exemption, so the tax saving pays for the difference." She is in the 30% slab under the old regime.
body.prompt: Is her friend right? Work out what the move does to her exemption and her finances.
body.modelAnswer: No. At ₹30,000 a month her annual rent of ₹3,60,000 already sits exactly at her rent ceiling: Limit 2 is ₹3,60,000 minus ₹72,000 = ₹2,88,000, equal to Limit 1, her full HRA. At ₹38,000 a month, Limit 2 rises to ₹4,56,000 minus ₹72,000 = ₹3,84,000, but Limit 1 stays at ₹2,88,000, so her exemption does not change at all. She would pay ₹96,000 more rent a year for zero extra tax saving. The move might still make sense for space or comfort, but tax is not a reason for it.

children.text: The Five-Step Method

cells: Use the months in which you lived in the rented home and received HRA
Basic, plus DA if your terms of employment provide for it, plus fixed-percentage commission
HRA received; rent minus 10% of salary; 50% or 40% of salary

body.text: Working in monthly figures and multiplying by 12 gives the right answer only when salary, HRA, rent and city stay the same all year. If any of them change, work the limits out separately for each period with different figures. Lesson 8 shows how.

children.text: Your Turn

body.title: Try It: Sunil in Kolkata
body.prompt: Sunil works in Kolkata and rents a flat in Salt Lake for ₹32,000 a month. His basic salary is ₹70,000 a month and his HRA is ₹35,000 a month. He has no DA or commission and is on the old regime. What is his annual exempt HRA for tax year 2026-27? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Salary is ₹8,40,000. Limit 1: ₹4,20,000. Limit 2: ₹3,84,000 minus ₹84,000 = ₹3,00,000. Limit 3: 50% of ₹8,40,000 = ₹4,20,000. The smallest is Limit 2, so ₹3,00,000 is exempt and ₹1,20,000 is taxable.

body.title: Try It: Sunil's Rent Ceiling
body.prompt: Using the same figures, what is the highest monthly rent at which every extra rupee of rent still increases Sunil's exemption? Answer in rupees per month.
body.explanation: The ceiling is the smaller of Limit 1 and Limit 3, plus 10% of salary. Both Limit 1 and Limit 3 are ₹4,20,000. Adding ₹84,000 gives ₹5,04,000 a year, which is ₹42,000 a month. Sunil pays ₹32,000, so he is ₹10,000 a month below his ceiling.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Low-Rent Trap
body.textWithBlank: If your annual rent is less than or equal to 10% of your salary, your HRA exemption is ___.
body.explanation: Limit 2 becomes zero or negative, and because the exemption is the smallest of the three limits, it is zero. All your HRA is then taxable, even though you pay rent.

body.title: Run the Three Limits on Your Own Salary
steps: Write down your monthly basic, eligible DA, HRA and rent from your payslip and rent agreement
Check whether the city of your rented home is on the eight-city list to pick 50% or 40%
Multiply by 12 if nothing changed during the year, otherwise split the year into periods
Calculate Limit 1, Limit 2 and Limit 3, and circle the smallest
Work out your rent ceiling and see how far above or below it you are
Compare your answer with the HRA exemption shown in your employer's tax computation sheet

cards.definition: The actual HRA received for the period. You can never exempt more HRA than you were paid.
Rent actually paid minus 10% of salary. The only limit that moves with your rent. Treated as zero if negative.
50% of salary if the rented home is in one of the eight listed cities, 40% elsewhere.
Whichever of the three limits is smallest. It sets your exemption, and only changing that limit can raise it.
HRA received minus exempt HRA. It is added to your salary and taxed at your slab rate.
The smaller of Limit 1 and Limit 3, plus 10% of salary. Rent above this level does not increase your exemption.

points: Exempt HRA is the smallest of HRA received, rent minus 10% of salary, and 50% or 40% of salary, all for the same period
The smallest limit is your binding limit and tells you what is capping your exemption
Rent below 10% of salary gives a zero exemption, so every rupee of HRA is taxed
Above your rent ceiling, extra rent adds nothing to the exemption. Below it, each rupee of extra rent saves at most 31.2 paise
Monthly figures multiplied by 12 work only when nothing changes during the year
Taxable HRA is simply HRA received minus the exempt amount, and it is taxed with the rest of your salary
